title: MemoryBench: A Benchmark for Memory and Continual Learning in LLM Systems
claim: A system's memory decomposes into distinct types, each updated from different kinds of user feedback given on a task.
layout: 2 columns, left-to-right; dialogue bubbles feed nested green memory boxes via arrows
description: The left column is a dialogue between a user icon and an AI. A legal question about a Chinese company is followed by an AI answer. A third bubble holds the user's verbal feedback, which points out an error, and below it action feedback icons: thumbs up, thumbs down, copy and a power or regenerate button. The thumbs-down is dark and the others are greyed. On the right, a large green rounded box holds dashed green sub-boxes. Declarative Memory contains Semantic Memory, which has a legal-article fact, and Episodic Memory, which has facts about the user. Procedural Memory sits below and says how to improve judgment documents. Arrows run from the feedback into the memory boxes. Dark green headings and gold feedback labels draw the eye first.
caption: An illustrative example of different types of memory and user feedback.
abstract: Scaling up data, parameters, and test-time computation has been the mainstream methods to improve LLM systems (LLMsys), but their upper bounds are almost reached due to the gradual depletion of high-quality data and marginal gains obtained from larger computational resource consumption. Inspired by the abilities of human and traditional AI systems in learning from practice, constructing memory and continual learning frameworks for LLMsys has become an important and popular research direction in recent literature. Yet, existing benchmarks for LLM memory often focus on evaluating the system on homogeneous reading comprehension tasks with long-form inputs rather than testing their abilities to learn from accumulated user feedback in service time. Therefore, we propose a user feedback simulation framework and a comprehensive benchmark covering multiple domains, languages, and types of tasks to evaluate the continual learning abilities of LLMsys. Experiments show that the effectiveness and efficiency of state-of-the-art baselines are far from satisfying, and we hope this benchmark could pave the way for future studies on LLM memory and optimization algorithms. Website: https://memorybench.thuir.cn Code: https://github.com/THUIR/MemoryBench Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/THUIR/MemoryBench Data-Full: https://huggingface.co/datasets/THUIR/MemoryBench-Full
